title: The Race to Nome

p: A

In January of 1925, a doctor in Nome, Alaska sent an urgent telegram. Children in his town were sick with diphtheria. Without medicine, the disease could kill most of them. The nearest supply was a thousand miles away.
B
Nome was frozen in. The port was iced over until spring. The two airplanes in the territory had open cockpits and engines that would not start in the cold. That left one way in: dog sled.
C

The plan was a relay. The medicine traveled by train as far as the rails went, to a town called Nenana. From there, twenty mushers and about 150 sled dogs would carry it in stages across 674 miles of frozen Alaska.
D

The weather was brutal. Temperatures dropped near sixty degrees below zero. One musher, Leonhard Seppala, took a shortcut straight across the frozen sea ice of Norton Sound during a blizzard. If the ice had broken, his whole team would have gone into the water.
E

The final stretch belonged to a musher named Gunnar Kaasen and his lead dog, Balto. Wind flipped the sled and buried the package of medicine in the snow. Kaasen dug it out with his bare hands. He reached Nome on the morning of February 2nd.
F

The relay took five and a half days. The medicine arrived frozen but unbroken. A statue of Balto still stands in Central Park in New York, and every year the Iditarod sled dog race follows part of the same trail.

Why could the medicine not be flown or shipped to Nome?
It could not be shipped because the port was frozen over until spring, and it could not be flown because the only two airplanes had open cockpits and engines that would not start in the cold.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. trapped) and paragraph E (i.e. Balto).
summarize
Summarize how the medicine reached Nome.

vocabulary

relay: A relay is when a team takes turns, each member carrying something part of the way.
connection
Describe the connection between the weather and the danger the mushers faced.
Because temperatures were near sixty below and a blizzard was blowing, the mushers risked frostbite, and Seppala risked breaking through the sea ice with his entire team.

title: Why Your Stomach Growls

p: A
You are sitting in a quiet classroom and your stomach makes a long, loud noise. Everyone hears it. The sound has less to do with hunger than you might think.
B

Your stomach and intestines are muscular tubes. About every ninety minutes, whether you have eaten or not, those muscles squeeze in a wave that pushes everything forward. The wave is called peristalsis. It works the way you squeeze toothpaste out of a tube.
C

Inside those tubes there is always some liquid and some gas. When the muscles squeeze, the gas and liquid get pushed through narrow spaces. That is what makes the sound. Your body is not empty and rumbling. It is full and moving.
D

So why does it seem louder when you are hungry? There are two reasons. Food muffles the noise, the way a full water bottle sloshes less than an empty one. And when you have not eaten for a couple of hours, your body runs an extra strong wave to sweep out leftovers.
E
A growling stomach is not a problem to fix. It is a sign that the machinery is running.
A

B
Your stomach and intestines are tubes made of muscle. About every ninety minutes those muscles squeeze in a wave. The wave pushes everything forward, like squeezing a tube of toothpaste.
C
There is always some liquid and some gas inside the tubes. When the muscles squeeze, the gas and liquid get pushed through tight spaces. That is the sound you hear.
D

Why is it louder when you are hungry? Food muffles the sound, the way a full water bottle sloshes less than an empty one. Also, when you have not eaten in a while, your body runs an extra strong wave to sweep out leftovers.

A growling stomach is not a problem. It means your body is working.

qs: main idea/detail
Why does a stomach with food in it make less noise?
A stomach with food in it makes less noise because the food muffles the sound, the way a full water bottle sloshes less than an empty one.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. squeezing) and paragraph D (i.e. hunger).
summarize
Summarize what causes the sound of a growling stomach.

The stomach and intestines squeeze in waves about every ninety minutes. Those squeezes push gas and liquid through narrow spaces, and that makes the growling sound. It is louder when you are hungry because there is no food to muffle it.
vocabulary

peristalsis: Peristalsis is the wave of squeezing that pushes food through your stomach and intestines.
muffles: Muffles means makes a sound quieter. Food in the stomach makes the noise quieter.
connection
Describe the connection between an empty stomach and a louder growl.
Because there is no food to muffle the sound and the body runs an extra strong cleaning wave, an empty stomach growls louder than a full one.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the muscles squeeze every ninety minutes" or "there is always gas and liquid inside." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: The Hats That Almost Ended the Birds

p: A
In the 1890s, the most fashionable hats in America were covered in feathers. Not small feathers. Whole wings. Sometimes an entire stuffed bird sat on the brim.
B

The demand was enormous. Hunters shot herons, egrets, and terns by the millions. Egrets were hunted hardest, because their finest feathers grow only during nesting season. Killing the adults left the chicks to starve. Some species came close to disappearing.
C

Two women in Boston, Harriet Hemenway and Minna Hall, decided to act. Neither could vote. So they used what they did have: an invitation list. They asked the wealthiest women in the city to tea and asked them to stop wearing feathers.
D
It worked. Hundreds agreed. The group they formed became the Massachusetts Audubon Society. Similar groups appeared in other states, and together they pushed for laws.
E

In 1918, Congress passed a law making it illegal to hunt most wild birds for their feathers. Egret populations recovered. The next time you see a snowy egret standing in shallow water, remember that it is there partly because of a tea party.
A
In the 1890s, the most stylish hats in America were covered in feathers. Some hats had whole wings on them. Some had a whole stuffed bird.
B

Hunters shot millions of birds to sell the feathers. Egrets were hunted the most. Their best feathers only grow during nesting season, so killing the adults left the chicks to starve. Some birds almost disappeared.
C
Two women in Boston decided to act. Their names were Harriet Hemenway and Minna Hall. Neither one could vote. So they invited rich women to tea and asked them to stop wearing feathers.
D
It worked. Hundreds agreed. The group became the Massachusetts Audubon Society. Groups in other states pushed for laws.
E
In 1918, Congress made it illegal to hunt most wild birds for their feathers. The egrets came back.

qs: main idea/detail
Why were egrets hunted harder than other birds?
Egrets were hunted hardest because their finest feathers grow only during nesting season, so hunters killed the adult birds while they had chicks.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. tea) and paragraph E (i.e. law).
summarize
Summarize how the feather trade was stopped.

Two women in Boston invited wealthy women to tea and asked them to stop wearing feathers. Hundreds agreed, and their group became the Massachusetts Audubon Society. Groups like it pushed for laws, and in 1918 Congress made hunting wild birds for feathers illegal.
vocabulary

demand: Demand means how much people want to buy something. So many people wanted feathered hats that hunters killed millions of birds.
recovered: Recovered means got better and grew back. The egret population grew again after the law passed.
connection
Describe the connection between nesting season and the danger to egret chicks.
Because the finest feathers grew only during nesting season, hunters killed the adult egrets while they had chicks, and the chicks starved without their parents.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "neither woman could vote" or "similar groups formed in other states." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: Cities Under Our Feet

p: A
Step on a sidewalk crack in summer and there is a good chance you are standing over a city. Ant colonies can run for yards underground, with rooms, roads, and jobs.
B

A colony begins with a single queen. After her mating flight she lands, breaks off her own wings, digs a small chamber, and lays her first eggs. She feeds those first larvae using her wing muscles, which she will never need again.
C
Once workers hatch, they take over. Some dig. Some forage for food. Some care for the young. Some do almost nothing for days at a time, which scientists think is a reserve crew for emergencies.
D

The rooms have purposes. There are nurseries held at a steady temperature, food storage rooms, and a waste room kept far from everything else. Leafcutter ants add a farm room where they grow a fungus on chewed leaves. The fungus, not the leaves, is their food.
E

No ant is in charge. The queen lays eggs; she does not give orders. Each ant follows simple rules and responds to chemical signals from its neighbors. Out of thousands of small decisions, a city runs.
A
Step on a sidewalk crack and you may be standing over a city. Ant colonies run for yards underground. They have rooms, roads, and jobs.
B
A colony starts with one queen. She lands, breaks off her own wings, digs a small room, and lays her first eggs.
C
Once workers hatch, they take over. Some dig. Some look for food. Some care for the young. Some rest, and scientists think they are a backup crew.
D
The rooms have jobs. There are nurseries, food rooms, and a trash room kept far away. Leafcutter ants even grow a fungus on chewed leaves and eat that.
E
No ant is the boss. The queen lays eggs but gives no orders. Each ant follows simple rules and signals from its neighbors. That is how the city runs.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the queen use to feed her very first larvae?
The queen feeds her first larvae using her own wing muscles, which she no longer needs after she breaks off her wings.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. rooms) and paragraph E (i.e. rules).
summarize
Summarize how an ant colony is organized.

One queen starts the colony and lays all the eggs. Workers then dig, forage, and care for the young. The colony has separate rooms for nurseries, food, and waste. No ant is in charge; each one follows simple rules and chemical signals.
vocabulary

forage: Forage means to go out and search for food.
colony: A colony is a large group of ants that live and work together in one nest.
connection
Describe the connection between simple rules and a working colony.
Because each ant follows simple rules and reacts to signals from its neighbors, thousands of small decisions add up, and the whole colony works without anyone in charge.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the waste room is kept far from everything else" or "leafcutter ants grow a fungus." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: The Glue That Failed

p: A
In 1968, a scientist named Spencer Silver was trying to invent a very strong glue. He failed. What he made instead was a glue that stuck lightly and peeled off without leaving a mark.
B
Silver thought it was useful. Nobody else did. For five years he gave talks inside his own company trying to find someone who wanted a weak glue. No one took it.
C
Then a coworker named Art Fry got annoyed at church. He sang in the choir, and the paper scraps he used to mark the hymns kept sliding out of his book. He remembered Silver’s glue.
D
Fry coated small pieces of paper with it. The markers stayed in the book, then peeled out clean. He made batches for people around the office, and those people would not stop asking for more.
E
The first stores barely sold any. So in 1980 the company mailed free samples to offices in one city. Nine out of ten people who tried them ordered more. The notes went on sale everywhere that year.
F
A glue that was too weak became one of the most common objects in the world. Silver had not failed. He had solved a problem nobody had asked about yet.

B
Silver thought it was useful. No one else did. For five years he looked for someone who wanted a weak glue. No one took it.
C
Then a coworker named Art Fry got annoyed at church. The paper he used to mark songs kept sliding out of his book. He remembered Silver’s glue.
D
Fry put the weak glue on small pieces of paper. The markers stayed in the book and peeled out clean. He made some for people in his office. They kept asking for more.
E

qs: main idea/detail
Why did Art Fry think of Spencer Silver’s glue?
Art Fry thought of the glue because the paper scraps he used to mark hymns in his choir book kept sliding out, and he needed a marker that would stay put and still peel off clean.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. rejected) and paragraph E (i.e. samples).
summarize
Summarize how a failed glue became a useful product.

Spencer Silver accidentally made a weak glue and could not find a use for it. Art Fry used it to make paper markers that stayed in his choir book and peeled off clean. After free samples convinced people to try them, the notes sold everywhere.
vocabulary

samples: Samples are free pieces of a product that a company gives away so people will try it.
batches: Batches are groups of something made at one time. Fry made groups of sticky notes for his coworkers.
connection
Describe the connection between the weak glue and the usefulness of the paper markers.
Because the glue was weak, the markers stuck in the book but peeled out without tearing the page, which is exactly what Fry needed.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "Silver spent five years looking for a use" or "nine out of ten people who got samples ordered more." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: The Town That Moved

p: A
Kiruna is a town in the far north of Sweden. It sits on top of the largest iron mine in the world. For a hundred years the mine has paid for the town. Now the mine is taking the town back.
B
Digging under Kiruna has made the ground unsteady. Cracks are spreading toward the buildings. Engineers say that if nothing is done, parts of the town will sink.
C
So Sweden decided to move the town. Not rebuild it somewhere else. Move it. Workers lift whole buildings onto trailers and drive them two miles east.
D
The church went first. It is more than a hundred years old and built of wood. Crews cut it into pieces, drove each piece down the road, and put it back together.
E

Not everything can travel. Most homes are being torn down and rebuilt instead. Families have been given apartments in the new center. Some people are glad. Others say the new town does not feel like home.
F
The move started in 2014 and will not finish until the 2030s. About six thousand people will end up with new addresses without ever leaving Kiruna.

B

C

D

Why does Kiruna have to move?
Kiruna has to move because digging in the iron mine underneath has made the ground unsteady, and cracks are spreading toward the buildings.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. moving) and paragraph E (i.e. feelings).
summarize
Summarize what is happening in Kiruna and why.

Mining under Kiruna made the ground unsafe, so Sweden is moving the whole town two miles east. Some buildings, like the wooden church, are cut apart and driven to the new site. Most homes are torn down and rebuilt. The move began in 2014 and will take until the 2030s.

unsteady: Unsteady means not firm or safe. The ground under Kiruna can shift and sink.
crews: Crews are teams of workers who do a job together.
connection
Describe the connection between the mine and the cracks in the ground.
Because the mine removes rock from underneath the town, the ground above has less holding it up, so it shifts and cracks.

title: The Dogs That Find Whales

p: A

Scientists who study killer whales have a problem. The whales live underwater. You cannot weigh one, check its health, or find out what it ate. Most of what a researcher wants to know is out of reach.
B
There is one exception. Whale scat, which is whale waste, floats for about half an hour before it sinks. A sample tells researchers what the whale ate, whether it is pregnant, and how stressed it is.
C
Finding it is the hard part. A boat crew scanning the water might spot one sample in a long day. So researchers turned to dogs.
D

A dog named Tucker was trained to smell whale scat from up to a mile away. He stood at the bow of the boat and leaned toward the scent. The crew steered wherever he leaned. When the boat got close, his body language changed, and the crew scooped the sample out of the water.
E

Dogs like Tucker found four times more samples than people scanning alone. What the samples showed mattered: these whales were not starving from a shortage of salmon, the way scientists had assumed. They were eating, but they were stressed by boat traffic.
F
The dogs never see a whale. They only smell what one left behind.
A

C
Finding it is hard. A crew watching the water might find one sample all day. So researchers used dogs.

Why do researchers want samples of whale scat?
A sample tells researchers what the whale ate, whether it is pregnant, and how stressed it is, which they cannot learn any other way.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. Tucker) and paragraph E (i.e. results).
summarize
Summarize how dogs help scientists study killer whales.

Killer whales are hard to study because they live underwater, but their floating scat holds useful information. Dogs trained to smell it from up to a mile away point the boat toward samples, and crews find four times more that way. The samples showed the whales were stressed by boat traffic rather than starving.

samples: Samples are small amounts collected so scientists can test and study them.
stressed: Stressed means under strain or pressure. Boat traffic put pressure on the whales.
connection
Describe the connection between the dogs and what scientists learned about the whales.
Because the dogs found four times more samples, scientists had enough evidence to see that the whales were eating but stressed by boat traffic, which changed what they had assumed.

title: How a Seed Crosses an Ocean

p: A
A new island rises out of the sea with no life on it at all. Within a few years, plants are growing there. They had to get there somehow, and plants cannot move.
B
Wind carries the smallest seeds. Orchid seeds are as fine as dust. A single pod releases millions of them, and a few ride the wind for hundreds of miles.
C
Birds carry others. A seed with a hook catches in feathers. A seed inside a berry gets eaten, rides in the bird’s gut for hours, and lands in a new place already surrounded by fertilizer.
D

The ocean carries the biggest travelers. A coconut has a thick husk full of air pockets, so it floats, sometimes for months. Salt water cannot get through the shell to the seed inside. Coconuts have crossed thousands of miles of open water and sprouted on beaches where no coconut palm had ever grown.
E
Not every traveler survives. Most seeds land in salt water or on bare rock and die. But a plant does not need most of its seeds to make it. It only needs one.
A
An island rises out of the sea with no life on it. Plants show up anyway. They cannot move, so how do they get there?
B
Wind carries the smallest seeds. Orchid seeds are as fine as dust. One pod lets out millions, and a few ride the wind for hundreds of miles.
C
Birds carry others. A seed with a hook sticks in feathers. A seed inside a berry gets eaten and lands far away in the bird’s waste.
D

The ocean carries the biggest seeds. A coconut has a thick husk full of air. It floats for months, and salt water cannot reach the seed inside. Coconuts have crossed thousands of miles and grown on new beaches.
E
Most seeds land in salt water or on bare rock and die. But a plant does not need most of its seeds to make it. It only needs one.

qs: main idea/detail
How does a coconut survive a long trip across the ocean?
A coconut has a thick husk full of air pockets so it floats, and the hard shell keeps salt water from reaching the seed inside.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. birds) and paragraph D (i.e. floating).
summarize
Summarize the three ways seeds travel to new places.

Wind carries dust-sized seeds like orchid seeds for hundreds of miles. Birds carry seeds that hook onto feathers or pass through their guts. The ocean floats big seeds like coconuts for months. Most seeds die on the way, but a plant only needs one to survive.
vocabulary

husk: A husk is the thick outer covering of a seed or fruit. The coconut husk is full of air pockets.
fertilizer: Fertilizer is material that helps plants grow. Bird droppings act as fertilizer around a seed.
connection
Describe the connection between the coconut husk and where coconut palms grow.
Because the air-filled husk lets a coconut float for months and the shell keeps salt water out, coconuts can drift thousands of miles and sprout on beaches where no palm grew before.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "orchid seeds are as fine as dust" or "a seed in a berry lands surrounded by fertilizer." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: The Woman Who Got Tired of Broken Dishes

p: A
Josephine Cochrane owned fine china that had been in her family for generations. In the 1880s she threw large dinner parties, and her servants kept chipping the plates while washing them.
B
She decided to wash them herself. She did not like that either. So she measured every dish she owned and built wire compartments shaped to hold each one.
C
Then she mounted the compartments in a wheel inside a copper boiler. A motor turned the wheel while a pump sprayed hot soapy water up from the bottom. In 1886 she received a patent for it.
D

Selling it turned out to be harder than building it. Families did not want one. Washing dishes by hand was cheap, and most homes could not make water hot enough. So Cochrane went to hotels and restaurants, where washing hundreds of plates by hand was slow and expensive. They bought.
E

Her machine won an award at the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago. She ran her company until she died in 1913. Home dishwashers did not become common until the 1950s, about seventy years after she built the first one.
A
Josephine Cochrane owned fine china that had been in her family for years. In the 1880s she had big dinner parties. Her servants kept chipping the plates while washing them.
B
She tried washing them herself. She did not like that either. So she measured every dish she owned and built wire holders shaped to fit each one.
C
She put the holders in a wheel inside a copper tub. A motor turned the wheel while a pump sprayed hot soapy water up from the bottom. In 1886 she got a patent.
D
Selling it was harder than building it. Families did not want one, because washing by hand was cheap. So she sold to hotels and restaurants, where washing hundreds of plates took a long time.
E
Her machine won an award at the 1893 World’s Fair. Home dishwashers did not become common until the 1950s.

qs: main idea/detail
Why did Cochrane sell her machine to hotels instead of to families?
She sold to hotels and restaurants because families found hand washing cheap and most homes could not make water hot enough, while hotels had hundreds of plates to wash and it was slow and expensive.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. machine) and paragraph D (i.e. selling).
summarize
Summarize how and why Josephine Cochrane invented the dishwasher.

Cochrane was tired of her servants chipping her family china. She measured her dishes, built a wire compartment for each one, and mounted them in a wheel inside a boiler with a pump that sprayed hot water. She patented it in 1886 and sold it to hotels and restaurants, which needed it more than families did.
vocabulary

compartments: Compartments are separate spaces that each hold one thing. Each dish had its own wire compartment.
patent: A patent is a legal document saying that an inventor owns the rights to an invention.
connection
Describe the connection between the chipped plates and the design of the machine.
Because plates were being chipped during hand washing, Cochrane measured every dish and built a compartment shaped to hold each one, so nothing could knock against anything else.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "she measured every dish she owned" or "her machine won an award in 1893." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: Why Bridges Have Gaps

p: A

Walk across a long bridge and at some point you will step over a metal comb set into the road. The teeth fit together but do not touch. That gap is not damage. It is one of the most important parts of the bridge.
B

Steel and concrete expand when they get hot and shrink when they get cold. The change is tiny for a short piece, but a bridge is not short. A steel span a mile long can grow more than a foot between a January night and a July afternoon.
C
If both ends were bolted down, that extra length would have nowhere to go. The bridge would push against its own supports with enormous force. Concrete would crack. Steel would buckle.
D

So engineers build in expansion joints. One end of the span rests on rollers or a sliding plate. The comb-shaped gap opens in winter and closes in summer, and the road stays smooth enough to drive over either way.
E

The same idea shows up in sidewalks, railroad tracks, and pipelines. Anything long and rigid that sits outside needs somewhere to put the extra length. Engineers do not fight the expansion. They plan a place for it to go.
A
Walk across a long bridge and you will step over a metal comb in the road. The teeth fit together but do not touch. That gap is not damage. It is important.
B
Steel and concrete grow when they get hot and shrink when they get cold. A bridge a mile long can grow more than a foot from a winter night to a summer day.
C
If both ends were bolted down, that growth would have nowhere to go. The bridge would push hard on its own supports. Concrete would crack. Steel would bend.
D
So engineers leave gaps called expansion joints. One end of the bridge rests on rollers. The gap opens in winter and closes in summer.
E
The same idea shows up in sidewalks, train tracks, and pipes. Anything long that sits outside needs a place to put the extra length.

qs: main idea/detail
What would happen if both ends of a long bridge were bolted down?
If both ends were bolted down, the extra length from expansion would have nowhere to go, so the bridge would push against its supports until the concrete cracked or the steel buckled.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. expansion) and paragraph D (i.e. joints).
summarize
Summarize why bridges are built with gaps in them.

Steel and concrete expand in heat and shrink in cold, and a mile-long span can grow more than a foot. Bolted at both ends it would crack or buckle, so engineers leave expansion joints where the extra length can go. The same idea is used in sidewalks, tracks, and pipelines.
vocabulary

expand: Expand means to get bigger or longer. Steel expands when it heats up.
rigid: Rigid means stiff and not able to bend easily. Bridges and rails are long and rigid.
connection
Describe the connection between heat and damage to a bridge with no gaps.
Because heat makes the steel and concrete grow longer, a bridge bolted at both ends would press against its supports with great force, and the concrete would crack or the steel would buckle.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "one end rests on rollers" or "the gap opens in winter." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: How a Cave Is Carved

p: A
A cave does not get dug out. It gets dissolved.
B

It starts with rain. As a raindrop falls it picks up a little carbon dioxide from the air, and it picks up more as it soaks through soil. That turns the water slightly acidic, like very weak lemon juice.
C

Next the water sinks into the ground and reaches limestone. Limestone is a soft rock made from ancient sea shells, and weak acid dissolves it the way water dissolves sugar. Over thousands of years, water trickling along one crack widens it into a passage.
D
Then the water table drops. The passage drains, and for the first time there is air inside. Now the cave is a room instead of a pipe.
E

Water still drips in from above, and each drop carries dissolved limestone. When a drop hangs from the ceiling, a little of that limestone stays behind. Drop after drop builds a stone icicle called a stalactite. What splashes on the floor builds a stalagmite pointing up.
F
A stalactite may grow about the thickness of a sheet of paper in a year. The formations in a large cave took longer to build than humans have existed.
A
A cave is not dug out. It is dissolved.
B
It starts with rain. A falling raindrop picks up carbon dioxide from the air and from the soil. That makes the water a weak acid.
C
The water sinks down and reaches limestone. Limestone is a soft rock made from old sea shells. Weak acid dissolves limestone. Over thousands of years, water trickling along a crack makes it wider.
D
Then the water drains away. Air fills the passage. Now the cave is a room.
E

Water still drips from above. Each drop carries a little dissolved limestone. When a drop hangs from the ceiling, some limestone stays behind. Drop after drop makes a stone icicle called a stalactite. What splashes down makes a stalagmite.
F
A stalactite may grow as thick as a sheet of paper in one year.

qs: main idea/detail
What makes rainwater able to dissolve solid rock?
Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide from the air and from the soil, which makes it slightly acidic, and weak acid dissolves limestone.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. dissolving) and paragraph E (i.e. building).
summarize
Summarize the steps that form a cave.

Rain picks up carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid. It sinks into limestone and slowly dissolves a crack into a passage. When the water table drops, the passage drains and fills with air. Dripping water then leaves limestone behind, building stalactites from the ceiling and stalagmites from the floor.
vocabulary

dissolves: Dissolves means breaks apart into a liquid until it disappears, the way sugar dissolves in water.
formations: Formations are the shapes built up inside a cave, such as stalactites and stalagmites.
connection
Describe the connection between the draining water and the cave filling with air.
Because the water table drops, the water drains out of the passage, and air moves into the empty space, turning a flooded pipe into an open cave room.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "limestone is made from ancient sea shells" or "a stalactite grows a paper’s thickness in a year." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: The Long Road of a Banana

p: A
A banana in a Michigan grocery store in February grew on a plant that has never felt frost. Getting it there takes about three weeks, and it is never allowed to ripen on its own.
B
First, workers cut the bunch while the bananas are still hard and green. A ripe banana would turn to mush on the trip.
C

Next the bunches are washed in tanks to remove the sticky sap, cut into the smaller clusters you see in stores, and boxed. The boxes go into a refrigerated ship held at about 56 degrees, cold enough to slow ripening but not cold enough to damage the fruit.
D
The ship takes one to two weeks. For the entire trip the bananas stay green and hard.
E

Then comes the part most people never hear about. At a warehouse near the store, the boxes go into a sealed room and the room is filled with a gas called ethylene. Bananas make this gas themselves as they ripen, so adding it starts the process on schedule. In three to eight days the fruit turns yellow.
F
Only then does the banana go to the store. The ripening did not happen on a farm. It happened in a room, on a timer, a few miles from you.

Why are bananas picked while they are still green and hard?
They are picked green because a ripe banana would turn to mush during the three-week trip to the store.

summarize
Summarize the trip a banana takes to reach the store.

Describe the connection between the ethylene gas and the color of the banana.

title: How a Broken Bone Heals

p: A
A bone is not a dry stick. It is living tissue with blood running through it. That is why it can repair itself and a chair leg cannot.
B
The moment a bone breaks, blood vessels inside it tear. Blood pools around the break and clots. Within hours that clot forms a soft collar around both ends, which is why a fresh break swells.
C

Over the next week, cells arrive and turn the clot into a soft callus made of collagen, the same stretchy material in your ears. The bone is joined now, but it would bend under weight. This is the stage the cast protects.
D

During the following weeks the body replaces the soft callus with a hard one. Cells lay down minerals, mostly calcium, until the bridge is real bone. By six to eight weeks most breaks can carry weight again.
E

Then comes the part that takes longest. The hard callus is a lumpy patch, thicker than the original bone. For months, sometimes years, the body shaves the outside down and rebuilds the inside along the lines of force the bone actually feels.
F
When that work is finished, an X-ray may show no sign that anything ever happened.
A
A bone is not a dry stick. It is alive and has blood running through it. That is why it can fix itself.
B
When a bone breaks, blood vessels inside it tear. Blood pools around the break and clots. In a few hours the clot forms a soft collar. That is why a new break swells.
C
Over the next week, cells turn the clot into a soft callus. The bone is joined, but it would bend under weight. That is why you wear a cast.
D
Over the next weeks the body makes the callus hard. Cells add minerals like calcium until it is real bone. By six to eight weeks most breaks can hold weight.
E
Then comes the slowest part. The hard patch is lumpy and too thick. For months the body shaves it down and rebuilds the inside.
F
When it is done, an X-ray may show no sign of the break.

qs: main idea/detail
Why does a fresh break swell?
A fresh break swells because torn blood vessels let blood pool around the break, and within hours that blood clots into a soft collar around both ends.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. soft) and paragraph D (i.e. hardening).
summarize
Summarize the stages of a bone healing.

Blood pools at the break and clots into a collar. Cells turn the clot into a soft callus that joins the bone but bends under weight. The body then adds minerals until the bridge is hard bone, usually within six to eight weeks. Finally it spends months reshaping the lumpy patch back to normal.
vocabulary

callus: A callus here is the patch of new material the body builds across a break to join the two pieces.
minerals: Minerals are substances such as calcium that the body uses to make bone hard.
connection
Describe the connection between the soft callus and the need for a cast.
Because the soft callus joins the bone but would bend under weight, the cast holds the pieces in place until the body replaces it with hard bone.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "collagen is the same material as in your ears" or "most breaks carry weight by eight weeks." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: How a Wildfire Starts and Stops

p: A
A fire needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and heat. Take away any one and it goes out. Everything firefighters do in a forest comes back to that.
B
The fuel builds up first, often for decades. Dead needles, fallen branches, and dry brush pile on the forest floor. A wet year grows more grass, which dies and adds to the pile.
C
Then comes the spark. Lightning starts some fires. People start most of them, usually by accident.
D

What happens next depends on the wind. Wind pushes flame into fresh fuel and heats that fuel before the flame arrives, so the fire moves faster and faster in one direction. A fire running uphill behaves the same way, because heat rises into the slope above it.
E

Firefighters cannot remove the oxygen and usually cannot remove the heat, so they remove the fuel. Crews cut and scrape a strip of bare dirt, called a fire line, ahead of the flames. When the fire reaches that line, there is nothing left to burn.
F
Sometimes crews light a fire on purpose, burning the fuel between the line and the wildfire before the wildfire gets there. It looks reckless. It is the same idea: get the fuel out of the way first.
A

B

C
Then comes the spark. Lightning starts some fires. People start most of them by accident.
D

Why do firefighters build a fire line instead of trying to cool the fire?
A fire needs fuel, oxygen, and heat. Crews cannot remove the oxygen and usually cannot remove the heat, so they scrape away the fuel and the fire has nothing left to burn.
paragraph focus
Paragraph D (i.e. wind) and paragraph E (i.e. fire line).
summarize
Summarize how a wildfire builds and how crews stop it.

Dead needles, branches, and brush pile up for decades as fuel. A spark from lightning or a person starts the fire, and wind or a slope pushes it into fresh fuel and speeds it up. Since crews cannot remove oxygen or heat, they scrape a bare fire line to take the fuel away, sometimes burning fuel on purpose first.
vocabulary

fuel: Fuel is anything a fire can burn, such as dead needles, branches, and dry brush.
reckless: Reckless means careless about danger. Lighting a fire on purpose looks reckless but is carefully planned.
connection
Describe the connection between wind and the speed of a fire.
Because wind pushes the flame into fresh fuel and heats that fuel before the flame arrives, the fuel catches sooner, so the fire moves faster and faster in one direction.

title: From Sand to Window Glass

p: A
The window you are looking through started as sand. Not beach sand exactly, but sand made mostly of quartz.
B

First the sand is mixed with two other powders. Soda ash lowers the melting point so the mix melts at a temperature a furnace can actually reach. Limestone keeps the finished glass from slowly dissolving in water.
C
Next the mixture goes into a furnace at about 2,900 degrees. The grains lose their shape and become a thick glowing liquid, closer to honey than to water.
D

Then comes the clever part. The liquid glass is poured onto a shallow bath of melted tin. Glass floats on tin and does not mix with it, and because the tin is perfectly flat, the glass spreads out perfectly flat too, on both sides at once. Before this method, window glass had to be ground and polished for hours.
E

The sheet cools as it travels down the bath and comes off solid but still hot. It then moves slowly through a long oven that cools it by degrees. Cooling too fast would leave stress locked inside, and the glass would shatter later for no clear reason.
F
At the end, a machine cuts the ribbon into panes. The whole trip, from sand to cut glass, runs without ever stopping.
A
The window you are looking through started as sand.
B
First the sand is mixed with two powders. Soda ash makes the mix melt at a lower heat. Limestone keeps the glass from slowly dissolving in water.
C
Next the mix goes into a furnace at about 2,900 degrees. The grains melt into a thick glowing liquid.
D

E
The sheet cools as it moves down the bath. Then it goes slowly through a long oven. Cooling too fast would leave stress in the glass, and it could shatter later.
F
At the end, a machine cuts the ribbon into panes.

Why is the liquid glass poured onto melted tin?
Glass floats on tin without mixing with it, and because the tin is perfectly flat, the glass spreads out perfectly flat on both sides at once instead of needing hours of grinding.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. melting) and paragraph E (i.e. cooling).
summarize
Summarize how sand becomes a window.

Sand is mixed with soda ash to lower the melting point and limestone to keep the glass from dissolving. The mix melts in a furnace near 2,900 degrees. The liquid is floated on melted tin so it spreads perfectly flat, cooled slowly in a long oven so it will not shatter later, and finally cut into panes.
vocabulary

furnace: A furnace is a chamber built to hold very high heat, hot enough here to melt sand.
stress: Stress here means hidden strain left inside the glass. Cooling too fast leaves stress that can crack it later.
connection
Describe the connection between cooling speed and glass breaking later.

title: Life in a Tide Pool

p: A
Twice a day the ocean pulls back and leaves puddles behind in the rocks. These puddles are tide pools, and each one is a small world that gets rebuilt every twelve hours.
B

Living there is hard. When the tide is out, the water heats up in the sun and gets saltier as it evaporates. A rainstorm can make it almost fresh. Then the tide returns and slams the pool with cold waves. An animal in a tide pool has to survive all of it.
C

Different animals solve the problem differently. A barnacle glues itself to the rock and seals its shell shut, trapping enough water inside to last until the tide comes back. A limpet clings so tightly with its muscular foot that waves cannot pry it loose.
D

A sea star has a weapon most animals do not. Hundreds of tiny tube feet on its underside grip the rock and also grip prey. A sea star can hold a mussel closed shut and pull, hour after hour, until the mussel tires and opens.
E

Tide pools are organized in zones. The highest pools dry out longest and hold the toughest animals. Lower pools stay wet nearly all the time and hold species that could not survive higher up. Walk down a rocky shore and the residents change every few feet.
A
Twice a day the ocean pulls back and leaves puddles in the rocks. These are tide pools. Each one is a small world rebuilt every twelve hours.
B

C
Animals solve the problem in different ways. A barnacle glues itself to the rock and shuts its shell, trapping water inside. A limpet clings so tightly with its foot that waves cannot pull it off.
D
A sea star has hundreds of tiny tube feet. They grip the rock and grip prey too. A sea star can pull on a mussel for hours until it tires and opens.
E
Tide pools are set in zones. The highest pools dry out the longest and hold the toughest animals. Lower pools stay wet and hold animals that could not live higher up.

qs: main idea/detail
Why is a tide pool a hard place for an animal to live?

When the tide is out the water heats up and gets saltier as it evaporates, rain can make it almost fresh, and then the returning tide slams it with cold waves. One animal has to survive all of those changes.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. holding on) and paragraph E (i.e. zones).
summarize
Summarize how tide pool animals survive.

Tide pool animals have to handle heat, changing saltiness, and crashing waves. A barnacle glues itself down and seals water inside its shell. A limpet clings with a strong foot. A sea star uses tube feet to grip rock and pull mussels open. Animals are sorted into zones by how much drying they can take.
vocabulary

evaporates: Evaporates means turns into a gas and goes into the air. As pool water evaporates, the salt left behind makes it saltier.
zones: Zones are bands or levels along the shore. Each zone stays wet for a different amount of time and holds different animals.
connection
Describe the connection between how long a pool stays dry and which animals live in it.
Because higher pools are out of the water longest, only animals that can survive heat, salt, and drying live there, while lower pools stay wet and hold species that could not last higher up.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "a barnacle seals water inside its shell" or "the highest pools hold the toughest animals." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: The Parts of a Volcano

p: A
A volcano is not just a mountain with fire in it. It is a delivery system, and every part has a job.
B
It starts deep underground with a magma chamber, a pocket of melted rock. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it pushes upward whenever it finds a way.
C

The way up is the conduit, a pipe running through the mountain. At the top of the conduit is the vent, the opening where material escapes. Some volcanoes have one main vent. Others have side vents opening partway down the slope.
D

The bowl around the vent is the crater. When an eruption empties the magma chamber, the ground above can collapse into the hole it left, forming a much larger pit called a caldera. Crater Lake in Oregon fills a caldera six miles wide.
E

What comes out depends on the magma. Runny magma flows out as lava and builds wide, gently sloped shields, like the volcanoes of Hawaii. Thick, sticky magma traps gas until the pressure blows it apart, sending up ash and rock and building the steep cone shape most people picture.
F
Geologists read those shapes backward. The shape of a volcano tells them what kind of eruption built it.
A
A volcano is not just a mountain with fire in it. Every part has a job.
B
It starts deep underground with a magma chamber, a pocket of melted rock. Magma is lighter than the rock around it, so it pushes up.
C

D
The bowl around the vent is the crater. When an eruption empties the chamber, the ground can fall into the hole and make a much bigger pit called a caldera.
E

What comes out depends on the magma. Runny magma flows as lava and builds wide, gentle slopes. Thick, sticky magma traps gas until the pressure blows it apart, sending up ash and building a steep cone.
F

qs: main idea/detail
Why do some volcanoes have gentle slopes and others have steep cones?
Runny magma flows out as lava and spreads into wide, gently sloped shields. Thick, sticky magma traps gas until pressure blows it apart, throwing out ash and rock that pile into a steep cone.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. pathway) and paragraph E (i.e. shape).
summarize
Summarize the parts of a volcano and what each one does.

A magma chamber underground holds melted rock that pushes upward. The conduit is the pipe it travels through, and the vent is the opening where it escapes. The crater is the bowl around the vent, and a caldera is the much larger pit left when the ground collapses into an emptied chamber.
vocabulary

conduit: A conduit is a pipe or channel that carries something through. In a volcano it carries magma up to the vent.
caldera: A caldera is the large pit left when the ground collapses into an emptied magma chamber.
connection
Describe the connection between an emptied magma chamber and a caldera.
Because the eruption drains the magma chamber, the rock above it has nothing holding it up, so the ground collapses into the empty space and leaves a pit far wider than the original crater.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "some volcanoes have side vents" or "Crater Lake fills a six-mile caldera." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: How Birds Migrate

p: A

Every fall, billions of birds leave the places where they hatched and travel toward warmer ground. The Arctic tern makes the longest trip of any animal, flying from the Arctic to Antarctica and back, roughly 44,000 miles a year.
B

Birds migrate because food moves, not because they dislike cold. A warbler that eats insects has nothing to eat in a frozen northern forest. Chickadees, which can find seeds and dormant insects under bark, stay all winter.
C

Finding the way is the harder problem. Birds navigate using several tools at once. Many read the position of the sun, correcting for the time of day. Night migrants use the stars, and young birds appear to learn the pattern of rotation around the North Star before they ever fly.
D

Birds also sense the Earth’s magnetic field. The strength and angle of that field change as you move north or south, which gives a bird something like a built-in latitude reading. Landmarks help too: rivers, coastlines, and mountain ranges act as highways.
E

Migration is expensive. Small birds nearly double their weight in fat before leaving, then burn it in flights that can last more than sixty hours without landing. Many do not survive the trip. Enough do that the whole pattern repeats the next year.

Summarize why birds migrate and how they find their way.

Birds migrate because the food they eat disappears in winter. They navigate with several tools at once: the position of the sun, the pattern of stars around the North Star, the Earth’s magnetic field, and landmarks like rivers and coastlines. They fuel the trip by nearly doubling their weight in fat.
vocabulary

migrate: Migrate means to travel from one region to another at the same time each year, and then back again.
navigate: Navigate means to find and follow the right route to a place.
connection
Describe the connection between what a bird eats and whether it migrates.
Because a warbler eats insects that vanish from a frozen forest, it has to leave, while a chickadee can find seeds and dormant insects under bark, so it has no reason to go.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "the Arctic tern flies 44,000 miles a year" or "small birds nearly double their weight in fat." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: Deserts Are Not Always Hot

p: A
Most people picture a desert as hot sand. Heat is not what makes a desert. Dryness is.
B

A place counts as a desert if it is arid, meaning it receives less than about ten inches of precipitation in a year. Precipitation is any water that falls from the sky: rain, snow, sleet, or hail. By that measure the largest desert on Earth is Antarctica, which gets about two inches a year, almost all of it as snow.
C

Deserts form for different reasons. Some sit in the rain shadow of a mountain range: air rising over the mountains drops its moisture on the near side and arrives dry on the far side. Others sit under bands of sinking air that hold no rain. Antarctica is dry because cold air cannot hold much moisture in the first place.
D

Only about a fifth of the world’s deserts are covered in sand. The rest are gravel, bare rock, or salt flats. Where there is sand, wind piles it into dunes that move a few yards a year as grains blow up the gentle side and tumble down the steep one.
E
Desert plants survive by storing water, growing shallow roots that catch rain quickly, or waiting. Some seeds can sit in dry soil for years and sprout within days of a single storm.

B

C

D

Summarize what makes a place a desert.

title: What Makes an Earthquake

p: A
The outer shell of the Earth is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. They float on hotter, softer rock below and move about as fast as your fingernails grow.
B

Where two plates meet, there is a crack called a fault. The plates try to slide past each other along the fault, but rock is rough, and friction locks the two sides together. The plates keep pushing anyway, and the rock near the fault bends and stores the strain, like a stick you are slowly bending.
C
Eventually the friction gives. The two sides snap past each other in seconds, the bent rock springs back, and all the stored energy is released at once. That release is the earthquake.
D

The energy travels outward as seismic waves. Some waves push and pull the ground the way sound moves through air. Others shake it side to side. A seismograph records the waves as a jagged line, and the height of that line tells scientists how much energy was released.
E
The spot underground where the rock slips is the focus. The point on the surface directly above it is the epicenter, and that is usually where shaking is strongest.
F
Faults do not stop moving after a quake. They lock again and begin storing strain for the next one.

Paragraph B (i.e. strain) and paragraph E (i.e. location).

Summarize what causes an earthquake.

Because the bending rock stores energy the whole time the fault stays locked, all of it is released in the instant the rock finally slips, so the longer the strain builds the more energy the quake can release.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "plates move as fast as fingernails grow" or "a seismograph draws a jagged line." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: Inside a Beehive

p: A
A beehive looks like chaos. It is one of the most organized places in nature.
B
Every hive has one queen. She does one job: she lays eggs, up to two thousand a day in summer. She does not give orders. The hive runs without a boss.
C

Almost every other bee is a female worker, and her job changes as she ages. For her first days she cleans cells. Then she feeds larvae. Then she builds wax comb. Only in the last part of her life does she leave the hive to gather nectar.
D

Foragers share what they find by dancing. A bee that has located flowers runs in a figure eight on the comb. The angle of the run tells the other bees the direction relative to the sun, and the length of the waggle tells them how far.
E
The male bees, called drones, do no work at all. They cannot sting and cannot feed themselves. In fall the workers push them out of the hive.
F
Through winter the workers cluster around the queen and shiver their flight muscles, holding the center near 95 degrees while snow sits on the roof.
A

Use the index. You want to know how bees stay warm in cold weather. Which pages should you turn to, and why?
Pages 31–33, listed under "Winter cluster." That entry matches the topic of bees keeping warm in winter.

Paragraph C (i.e. jobs) and paragraph D (i.e. dancing).

Summarize how work is divided in a beehive.

title: The Layers of the Rainforest

p: A
A rainforest is not one habitat. It is four stacked on top of each other, and most animals spend their whole lives in just one.
B
The top layer is the emergent layer, where a few giant trees push above everything else. Up there the wind is strong and the sun is harsh. Eagles nest in it.
C

Below that is the canopy, a roof of branches so thick it blocks most of the light. This is the crowded layer. Roughly half of all rainforest species live here, including monkeys that can travel for miles without touching the ground.
D
The understory sits in shade. Plants there grow enormous leaves to catch what little light gets through, and the air stays still and humid.
E

The forest floor is the darkest. Only about two percent of sunlight reaches it. Little grows, but the floor is where everything breaks down. A fallen leaf rots in about six weeks, compared with a year in a forest farther north.
F
That fast breakdown is why rainforest soil is surprisingly thin. Nutrients do not build up in the ground; they go straight back into the trees.

Use the headings. Which one would you read to learn about monkeys, and how do you know?
Heading 2, "The Canopy: Where Half the Species Live." The canopy is the crowded layer where monkeys travel through the branches.

Paragraph C (i.e. crowded) and paragraph E (i.e. dark).

Summarize the four layers of a rainforest.

title: Reading a Weather Map

p: A
A weather map is packed with symbols, and once you know four of them you can predict tomorrow reasonably well.
B

The big letters come first. An H marks high pressure, where air is sinking. Sinking air does not form clouds, so an H usually means clear skies. An L marks low pressure, where air rises, cools, and forms clouds. An L usually means rain.
C

The lines with triangles and half circles are fronts, the boundaries where two air masses meet. Blue triangles mark a cold front: cold air shoving under warm air, which lifts it fast and can build thunderstorms in an hour. Red half circles mark a warm front: warm air sliding up over cold, which brings steady rain for longer.
D

Thin curving lines without symbols are isobars. Each one connects places with the same air pressure. When isobars are packed close together, the pressure changes sharply over a short distance, and that means wind.
E
Colors usually show precipitation on radar, from green for light rain to red for heavy.
F
Put those together and a map stops being decoration. It becomes a forecast you can read yourself.
A
A weather map is full of symbols. Once you know four of them, you can guess at tomorrow.
B
An H marks high pressure, where air sinks. That usually means clear skies. An L marks low pressure, where air rises and forms clouds. That usually means rain.
C

Lines with triangles or half circles are fronts, where two air masses meet. Blue triangles mean a cold front, which can build storms fast. Red half circles mean a warm front, which brings steady rain.
D
Thin curving lines are isobars. Each one connects places with the same air pressure. When they are packed close, expect wind.
E
Colors show rain on radar, from green for light to red for heavy.
F
Put those together and a map becomes a forecast you can read yourself.

qs: main idea/detail
Use the key. A map shows an L over your town with isobars packed tightly around it. What kind of day should you expect?
A rainy, windy day. The L means rising air and clouds, and tightly packed isobars mean the pressure changes sharply, which brings wind.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. fronts) and paragraph D (i.e. wind).
summarize
Summarize what the four main weather map symbols tell you.

H marks high pressure and sinking air, so clear skies. L marks low pressure and rising air, so clouds and rain. Fronts show where air masses meet, with cold fronts building storms fast and warm fronts bringing steady rain. Isobars connect equal pressure, and packed isobars mean wind.

fronts: A front is the boundary where two different air masses meet.
isobars: Isobars are lines on a map connecting places that have the same air pressure.
connection
Describe the connection between a cold front and a sudden storm.
Because cold air shoves underneath warm air and lifts it fast, clouds build quickly, so a cold front can produce a thunderstorm within an hour.

title: The Road to the Vote

p: A
When the United States began, most states allowed only white men who owned property to vote. Widening that circle took nearly two hundred years and a great deal of argument.
B
Property rules fell first. By the 1850s most states had dropped them, so a white man could vote whether or not he owned land.
C

After the Civil War, the Fifteenth Amendment said a state could not deny the vote because of race. In practice, poll taxes, literacy tests, and outright threats kept most Black citizens in the South from voting for another ninety years.
D

Women organized for seventy years before winning the vote. The Nineteenth Amendment passed in 1920, and it came down to a single vote in the Tennessee legislature, cast by a young man whose mother had written to him asking him to support it.
E

The Voting Rights Act of 1965 finally banned the tests and sent federal officials to register voters in places that had blocked them. Registration in Mississippi went from about 7 percent of Black adults to nearly 60 percent in four years.
F
In 1971 the voting age dropped from 21 to 18, driven by men being drafted at an age when they could not vote.
A
When the United States began, most states let only white men who owned property vote. Widening that circle took almost two hundred years.
B
Property rules fell first. By the 1850s most states had dropped them.
C

After the Civil War, the Fifteenth Amendment said a state could not deny the vote because of race. But poll taxes, reading tests, and threats kept most Black citizens in the South from voting for ninety more years.
D
Women organized for seventy years before winning the vote in 1920. It came down to a single vote in Tennessee.
E
The Voting Rights Act of 1965 banned the tests. In Mississippi, Black voter registration went from about 7 percent to nearly 60 percent in four years.
F
In 1971 the voting age dropped from 21 to 18.

qs: main idea/detail
Use the timeline. How many years passed between the Fifteenth Amendment and the Voting Rights Act?
Ninety-five years, from 1870 to 1965. The amendment banned denial by race, but the tests and taxes were not outlawed until 1965.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. blocked) and paragraph E (i.e. enforcement).
summarize
Summarize how voting rights expanded in the United States.

At first only white men with property could vote. Property rules fell by the 1850s. The Fifteenth Amendment banned denial by race in 1870, though tests and taxes blocked Black voters for ninety more years. Women won the vote in 1920, the Voting Rights Act enforced the earlier promise in 1965, and the age dropped to 18 in 1971.
vocabulary

amendment: An amendment is a change added to the Constitution.
register: To register is to sign up officially so that you are allowed to vote.
connection
Describe the connection between the Voting Rights Act and the change in Mississippi.

Because the act banned literacy tests and sent federal officials to sign people up, the barriers that had kept Black citizens off the rolls were removed, and registration rose from about 7 percent to nearly 60 percent in four years.

title: What Lives in the Deep Ocean

p: A
Sunlight runs out about 650 feet down. Below that is the largest habitat on Earth, and almost none of it has ever been seen.
B

The pressure is the first problem. It increases by about one atmosphere every 33 feet, so two miles down a body is squeezed by the weight of roughly 300 atmospheres. Deep sea animals survive it because they have no air pockets to crush. Their bodies are mostly water, which barely compresses.
C
Food is the second problem. Nothing grows without light, so most of the deep depends on "marine snow," a slow drift of dead material falling from above. It can take weeks to reach the bottom.
D

Many deep sea animals make their own light, a trick called bioluminescence. A chemical reaction in their bodies produces a cold glow. They use it to lure prey, to startle predators, and to find mates in the dark.
E

In the 1970s scientists found something that broke the rules: hot vents on the sea floor where whole communities live without sunlight at all. Bacteria there make food from the chemicals in the vent water, and tube worms, crabs, and clams live off them.
A
Sunlight runs out about 650 feet down. Below that is the largest habitat on Earth, and almost none of it has been seen.
B
Pressure is the first problem. It grows the deeper you go. Deep sea animals survive because they have no air pockets to crush. Their bodies are mostly water.
C
Food is the second problem. Nothing grows without light, so most of the deep lives on "marine snow," dead material drifting down from above.
D
Many deep sea animals make their own light. A chemical reaction makes a cold glow. They use it to catch food and to find mates.
E
In the 1970s scientists found hot vents on the sea floor. Whole communities live there without sunlight. Bacteria make food from chemicals in the vent water.

qs: main idea/detail
Use the diagram. At 5,000 feet, which zone are you in, and what is the light like?
The midnight zone, which runs from 3,300 to 13,000 feet. It is fully dark, so animals there rely on marine snow drifting down.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. food) and paragraph E (i.e. vents).
summarize
Summarize how animals survive in the deep ocean.

They handle crushing pressure because their bodies are mostly water and have no air pockets. Most feed on marine snow drifting down, since nothing grows without light. Many make their own light to lure prey and find mates. At hot vents, bacteria make food from chemicals and support whole communities.
vocabulary

pressure: Pressure is the weight of the water pressing in from every side. It grows the deeper you go.
bioluminescence: Bioluminescence is light made by a living thing through a chemical reaction in its body.
connection
Describe the connection between having no air pockets and surviving deep pressure.

Because pressure crushes air but barely compresses water, an animal whose body is mostly water and holds no air pockets has nothing for the pressure to squeeze, so it survives depths that would collapse an air-filled body.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "marine snow takes weeks to reach the bottom" or "vents were found in the 1970s." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: Homework in Elementary School

p: A
I taught third grade for eleven years, and I stopped assigning homework in my fourth year. I want to explain why, because I know not everyone agrees.
B

The research on elementary homework is thin. Studies find little connection between homework in the early grades and how much students learn. The connection gets stronger in high school, but that is not who I teach.
C

What I did see was the cost. Homework arrived finished for the students whose parents had time to sit down with them, and unfinished for the students whose parents worked nights. The assignment measured the household, not the child.
D
I replaced it with one request: read for twenty minutes, anything you like. No log, no signature. Reading volume is one thing that does predict how well children read later.
E

Some families were unhappy. They said homework builds discipline and prepares children for middle school. I understand that argument. I think eight-year-olds build discipline in other ways, and I would rather they spend the evening at dinner or outside.
F
You may weigh these things differently than I do. That is a fair thing to do. What matters is knowing which parts of what you just read were evidence and which were my opinion.
A
I taught third grade for eleven years. I stopped giving homework in my fourth year. I want to explain why.
B
Studies find little connection between homework in the early grades and how much students learn. The connection is stronger in high school, but that is not who I teach.
C
I also saw the cost. Homework came back finished for students whose parents had time to help, and unfinished for students whose parents worked nights.
D
I asked for one thing instead: read for twenty minutes, anything you like. How much a child reads does predict how well they read later.
E
Some families were unhappy. They said homework builds discipline. I understand that. I think eight-year-olds build discipline in other ways.
F
You may weigh these things differently than I do. That is fair.

qs: main idea/detail
What is the author’s point of view about homework, and what is her job?
The author is a third grade teacher of eleven years who believes elementary homework is not worth assigning. She replaced it with twenty minutes of free reading.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. unfairness) and paragraph E (i.e. disagreement).
summarize
Summarize the author’s reasons for dropping homework.

Research shows little connection between elementary homework and learning. The author also saw that finished homework tracked which families had free evenings rather than which children tried. She replaced it with free reading because reading volume does predict later reading ability.
vocabulary

discipline: Discipline here means the habit of doing work steadily even when you do not feel like it.
volume: Volume here means how much of something. Reading volume is how much a child reads.
connection
Describe the connection between a family’s schedule and whether homework came back finished.

Because homework was done at home, students whose parents were free in the evening got help finishing it, while students whose parents worked nights did not, so the grade reflected the household instead of the child.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "no log, no signature" or "the connection gets stronger in high school." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: Should Zoos Exist?

p: A
I work at a zoo, so you should know my point of view before you read further. I believe good zoos are worth keeping. I also think most people, including me, should be harder on the bad ones.
B

Here is the case against zoos. A tiger in the wild ranges over dozens of square miles. No enclosure comes close. Animals in small spaces often pace or rock, behaviors they do not show in the wild. Those are real problems and I am not going to argue them away.
C

Here is my case for zoos. Several species are alive today only because zoos bred them. The California condor was down to twenty-two birds in 1982. Every condor flying now descends from those twenty-two, raised in captivity and released.
D
Zoos also fund fieldwork. A share of every ticket at my zoo goes to protecting habitat in places most visitors will never see.
E
And zoos change people. It is hard to care about an animal you have only seen on a screen.
F

A reader could accept every fact in this article and still conclude that zoos should close. The facts are not the whole argument. What you think an animal is owed is the rest of it, and that part is yours.

I work at a zoo, so you should know my point of view before you read on. I believe good zoos are worth keeping.
B

D

Why does the author tell you where he works in the first sentence?
He works at a zoo, so he has a stake in the argument. He tells the reader up front so they can weigh his point of view while reading.

Paragraph B (i.e. against) and paragraph C (i.e. for).
summarize
Summarize the author’s position and the argument he admits is strong.

The author believes good zoos are worth keeping because zoo breeding saved species like the California condor, ticket money funds habitat protection, and seeing animals in person makes people care. He admits that no enclosure matches a wild animal’s range and that confined animals pace.

title: A Letter About the New Skate Park

p: A
To the editor: I have lived on Water Street for thirty-one years, and I am writing against the skate park proposed for the lot behind the fire station.
B
My reasons are practical. That lot has no parking. Skaters will park on Water Street, which is narrow enough that two cars already cannot pass when someone parks on both sides.
C
I also expect noise. Skateboards on concrete carry a long way, and the lot is forty feet from the nearest bedroom window, which is mine.
D
I want to be clear about what I am not saying. I am not saying teenagers are trouble. I hear that argument at every meeting and I think it is nonsense. The kids in this neighborhood shovel my walk.
E
I would support this park on the school property, where there is a parking lot already and no houses within two hundred feet. I have said so at three meetings.
F

A reader who does not live on a narrow street may weigh the parking problem differently than I do. A reader who skates certainly will. I am telling you where I stand and why, so you can decide what my reasons are worth.

title: Why I Changed My Mind About Wolves

p: A
I ranched cattle in Montana for twenty years, and for most of them I believed wolves should be shot on sight. I want to tell you what changed and what did not.
B
Wolves were removed from Yellowstone by 1926 and brought back in 1995. I opposed the return. I had lost calves to predators and I did not want more.
C

What changed my thinking was watching the park. Without wolves, elk had grazed the riverbanks bare. When wolves returned, elk stopped standing in the open bottoms, and willow and aspen grew back. Beavers followed the willows. Songbirds followed the trees.
D
I am not going to tell you wolves never take livestock. They do. I lost a heifer in 2011 and I was not philosophical about it.
E

What I changed my mind about is narrower than people assume. I now think wolves belong in wild country. I still think a rancher should be paid promptly for a confirmed kill, and I still think the people who argue loudest for wolves mostly do not live near any.
F
If you have never lost an animal, you may find my remaining objections too strong. If you ranch, you may find I gave up too much. Both of those are points of view, including mine.

title: Two Views of the Cell Phone Rule

p: A
Our district banned phones during the school day this year. Two people who live with that rule wrote about it.
B

A principal wrote: "I expected complaints and I got them, for about three weeks. Then the lunchroom got loud again, in a good way. Teachers report fewer arguments that started as group texts. I am aware that a rule which is convenient for adults is not automatically good for children, so we tracked it. Discipline referrals are down a fifth. I support the ban."
C

A seventh grader wrote: "I take the city bus home and my mom works until six. Before the ban I texted her when I got on. Now I cannot, and the office phone has a line. Adults keep saying we are addicted. Some kids are. I am trying to tell my mother I am safe."
D
Both of these people are describing the same rule honestly. Neither is making anything up.
E

They differ because they are standing in different places. The principal is responsible for three hundred students and measures the rule by what happens to all of them. The student is responsible for getting herself home.
F
A reader has to decide what weight to give each view. That decision is the reader’s, not the writers’.

title: The Oregon Trail

p: A
Between 1840 and 1869, roughly 400,000 people walked from Missouri to Oregon and California. The trail ran about 2,000 miles and took four to six months.
B
Timing mattered more than anything. Leave too early and there is no grass yet for the oxen. Leave too late and snow closes the mountains before you reach them. Most families left in April or May.
C
They walked. Wagons were packed with food and tools, not people, and were pulled by oxen rather than horses because oxen live on prairie grass and horses need grain.
D
The hardest stretches came last. By the time families reached the mountains, the oxen were thin and the food was low. Furniture was pushed off the trail to lighten the load.
E

F

title: Inside a Volcano Eruption

p: A
On May 18, 1980, the north face of Mount St. Helens slid off the mountain. It was the largest landslide ever recorded.
B

Pressure had been building for two months. Magma pushing up inside the mountain made the north slope swell outward about five feet per day. Scientists watched the bulge grow and knew something would give.
C
An earthquake at 8:32 that morning shook the bulge loose. The entire north face collapsed, and that removed the lid holding the pressure in.
D

What followed went sideways instead of up. A blast of superheated gas and rock shot north at hundreds of miles an hour, flattening forest for nineteen miles. Trees were laid down in rows all pointing away from the mountain.
E
Then the vertical column rose. Ash reached the stratosphere within fifteen minutes and fell on eleven states. In Yakima, Washington, streetlights came on at noon.
F
Fifty-seven people died. Life returned faster than expected: within five years, plants sprouted from roots that survived under the ash, and elk were grazing on the blast plain.

title: A Day in the Life of a Coral Reef

p: A
A coral reef is not a rock and it is not a plant. It is thousands of tiny animals called polyps, each one living inside a cup of limestone it built itself.
B

Each polyp holds algae inside its body. The algae make food from sunlight and share it with the polyp; the polyp gives the algae a safe place to live. That trade is why reefs grow only in shallow, clear water where light reaches.
C

The reef runs on a schedule. By day, parrotfish and surgeonfish graze algae off the coral, and the polyps stay closed. At dusk the day fish retreat into crevices and the polyps open, spreading tentacles to catch drifting plankton.
D
Night belongs to different hunters. Octopuses come out, and moray eels leave their holes to hunt sleeping fish.
E
When water gets too warm, the polyps expel their algae. The coral turns white, which is called bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead yet, but it is starving, and if the heat lasts it will die.
F
Reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor and shelter about a quarter of all ocean species.

title: How a City Gets Its Water

p: A
New York City drinks water that falls as rain a hundred miles away, and almost none of it is pumped. Gravity does the work.
B
It starts in the Catskill Mountains, where streams feed reservoirs built by flooding valleys. Several towns were bought and emptied to make room.
C
From the reservoirs, water enters tunnels bored through solid rock, some of them six hundred feet underground. The tunnels slope gently downhill the whole way, so the water keeps moving on its own.
D

Before it reaches taps, the water is treated. It is screened for debris, disinfected with ultraviolet light and chlorine, and fluoride is added. Most cities also filter their water; New York is one of the few large cities allowed to skip that step, because the land around its reservoirs is protected from development.
E
City Tunnel No. 3 has been under construction since 1970 and is still not finished. It is meant to let the older tunnels be shut off and inspected. Neither has been closed since it opened.
F
About a billion gallons a day arrive this way, without a single pump for most of the journey.

Summarize how water gets from the mountains to a city tap.

title: The Underground Railroad

p: A
The Underground Railroad was not underground and not a railroad. It was a network of people who helped enslaved men, women, and children escape north, and it used railroad words as code.
B
A conductor was a guide. A station was a house where someone could hide. A stationmaster was the person who lived there and risked everything by opening the door.
C

Most travel happened at night, often on foot, following creeks so dogs could not track a scent. The North Star pointed the way, and travelers who could not see it felt for moss on the north side of trees.
D
After 1850, escaping to a free northern state was no longer enough. A new federal law required officials in free states to return escapees, so many continued all the way to Canada.
E
Harriet Tubman escaped in 1849 and then went back into slave territory at least thirteen times to lead others out. She later said she never lost a passenger.
F
Nobody knows the true number. Historians estimate that tens of thousands reached freedom this way, though records were deliberately never kept.

title: Why Leaves Change Color

p: A
The red and orange in a fall leaf were there all summer. You just could not see them.
B
All summer, a leaf is full of chlorophyll, the green chemical that turns sunlight into food. There is so much of it that it hides every other color in the leaf.
C
Then the days get shorter. The tree senses the change in daylight, not the cold, and begins shutting the leaves down. It stops making new chlorophyll, and the green already there breaks apart.
D
As the green fades, the yellows and oranges underneath finally show. Those pigments were in the leaf the whole time, doing quiet work alongside the chlorophyll.
E

Red is different. Red is made fresh in the fall, and only in some trees. A bright red maple needs warm sunny days and cool nights to produce it, which is why the same tree looks brilliant one year and dull the next.
F
Finally the tree seals off each leaf at the stem. The leaf falls, and the tree spends the winter on food it stored while those leaves were still green.
