Summarize the steps that turn a green leaf into a fallen one.

title: The First Public Library

p: A
Two hundred years ago, owning books meant being wealthy. A single book could cost a week of a worker’s pay.
B

The first answer was the subscription library. Readers paid a yearly fee and shared a collection. This helped, but it only helped people who could afford the fee, which was the same people who could mostly afford books.
C
The idea that changed things was simple and strange at the time: a library paid for by taxes and free to everyone, whether they paid taxes or not.
D

People argued against it. Some said free books would make readers lazy. Others said taxpayers should not fund something they might never use. Supporters answered that a town full of readers is worth more than the tax, and that argument slowly won.
E
Boston opened the first large free public library in 1854. Anyone could walk in.
F

Between 1883 and 1929, Andrew Carnegie paid to build more than 1,600 library buildings in the United States, on one condition: the town had to promise to pay for the books and staff forever. He built the shell. The town had to mean it.

Summarize how free public libraries came to exist.

title: How Salmon Find Their River

p: A
A salmon hatches in a small freshwater stream, swims to the ocean, lives there for years, and then returns to the exact stream where it was born. Some travel two thousand miles to do it.
B

The journey out happens in stages. First the young salmon drifts downstream. Then, in the estuary where fresh water meets salt, its body rebuilds itself to survive in the ocean, a change that takes weeks.
C
Once at sea, it grows. A salmon spends one to five years in the ocean before the return trip begins.
D
Finding the way back uses two different tools. Far out at sea, the salmon reads the Earth’s magnetic field, which tells it roughly where the coast is. That gets it close, but not to the right stream.
E

Close to shore, it switches to smell. Every stream carries its own chemical signature from the rocks and plants around it, and the salmon memorized that smell as a young fish. It follows the scent upstream, choosing at every fork.
F
Then it spawns and dies. Its body decays in the stream, feeding the insects that its own young will eat the following spring.

title: Two Ways to Build a House

p: A
A house can be built on a site or built in a factory. Both end up looking like houses. Almost everything else is different.
B

A site-built house is assembled in place, in order. The foundation goes in, then the frame, then the roof, then everything inside. Each stage waits for the one before it, and all of it waits on weather.
C
A factory-built house is made in sections indoors. Walls are built flat on a table and stood up. Because the building is never rained on during construction, the wood never swells and dries.
D

Speed is the biggest difference. A factory house can be finished in weeks, because the foundation is poured at the site while the house itself is being built somewhere else. Two things happen at once instead of in line.
E
Site building wins on changes. If you decide halfway through that a room should be larger, a site crew can adjust. A factory section is already built.
F
Cost usually favors the factory, but not always. The sections have to be trucked to the site and lifted by crane, and a house going up a narrow mountain road can cost more to deliver than it saved.

title: What Happened to the Passenger Pigeon

p: A
In 1860 the passenger pigeon was probably the most numerous bird on Earth. A single flock could take three days to pass overhead and darken the sky while it did.
B
By 1914 there were none. The last one died in a zoo in Cincinnati.
C

Two things happened at the same time, and either alone might not have been enough. First, the forests were cut. Passenger pigeons ate beech and oak nuts, and those forests were cleared for farms across the eastern United States.
D

Second, they were hunted on a scale that is hard to picture. New railroads could carry barrels of pigeons to city markets, and the telegraph let hunters send word of where the flocks had landed. Nesting colonies were emptied in a few days.
E

Their own biology worked against them. Passenger pigeons nested in enormous colonies, which protected them by sheer numbers: a hawk could only eat so many. Below a certain size, that protection stopped working, and a small flock was worse off than a small flock of any ordinary bird.
F
That is why the collapse was so fast at the end. The species did not fade gradually. It fell off a cliff.

colony: A colony is a large group of animals that live and work together.
pollinators: Pollinators are animals that carry pollen between flowers so plants can make seeds.
connection
Describe the connection between dry pollen and better pollinating.
Because loose, dry pollen falls off a mason bee easily, more of it lands on the next flower she visits instead of staying packed on her body.
note: Students may choose many details, i.e. "workers share heat in winter" or "mason bee pollen is loose and dry." Check that the detail supports the main idea and is not an extraneous detail.

title: Two Texts: What Happened to the Dinosaurs

B

C
Around three quarters of all species on Earth disappeared, including every dinosaur except the group that became birds.
D
TEXT 2 · The asteroid is not the whole story. For about 300,000 years before the impact, enormous volcanoes in India were erupting almost without stopping.
E
Those eruptions poured gas into the air and changed the climate. Some scientists find that dinosaur numbers were already dropping before the asteroid arrived.
F
Most scientists now say both mattered. The volcanoes weakened life on Earth, and the asteroid finished it in a single afternoon.

title: Two Texts: Living on a Submarine

p: A
TEXT 1 · From a navy fact sheet. A submarine crew of 130 lives inside a steel tube for up to three months without surfacing.
B
Machines make oxygen from seawater and scrub carbon dioxide from the air. Fresh water is made from seawater too. Food is the only thing that runs out, and it sets the length of the trip.
C
There are fewer beds than sailors. Three sailors share two beds, taking turns by shift.
D
TEXT 2 · From a sailor’s interview. "The thing nobody tells you is that you stop knowing what time it is. There are no windows. The lights change color to tell you it is night."
E
"You run on an eighteen-hour day, six on and twelve off. Your body never quite agrees to it. After a month you stop arguing."
F
"The food matters more than you would think. When the fresh fruit runs out, around week three, everybody notices. That is the calendar."

B

Use both texts to explain why a patrol cannot last forever.

paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. supplying) and paragraph E (i.e. adjusting).
summarize
What is the most important point in each text?

Text 1 explains that machines supply the crew’s air and water, so only food limits the patrol. Text 2 explains what that life feels like: no windows, colored lights for night, an eighteen-hour day, and fruit gone by week three.
vocabulary

scrub: To scrub the air means to clean a gas out of it.
patrol: A patrol is one trip a submarine takes before returning to port.
connection
Describe the connection between having no windows and losing track of time.
Because there is no daylight to mark morning or evening, the crew has nothing to tell the hour by, so the ship changes the color of its lights to stand in for night.

title: Two Texts: The Great Wall

p: A
TEXT 1 · The Great Wall of China is not one wall. It is many walls, built by different rulers over 2,000 years, and later joined together.
B
The parts most visitors see were built in the 1400s and 1500s of brick and cut stone. Older sections, far to the west, were made of packed earth and have mostly worn away.
C
Together the walls run more than 13,000 miles, though no one ever walked the whole thing at once.
D
TEXT 2 · The Wall was built to stop riders from the north. It rarely did. Armies went around it, or paid a guard to open a gate.
E

What it did well was slow people down. A raider on horseback could cross the border in an hour. Getting a herd of stolen animals back over a wall took much longer, and that was long enough for soldiers to arrive.
F
The Wall also carried signal fires along its towers. A warning could travel hundreds of miles in a day, faster than any rider.

raider: A raider is someone who makes a quick attack to steal and then leave.
signal: A signal is a sign sent to pass a message, like a fire lit on a tower.
connection
Describe the connection between slowing raiders down and soldiers catching them.
Because stolen animals could not be hurried over a wall, the raiders lost hours getting back, and those hours were enough for soldiers who had seen the signal fires to reach them.

title: The Library That Rides a Donkey

p: A
In the mountains of Colombia, some villages have no road wide enough for a truck. Children there had no library until a teacher named Luis Soriano loaded books onto two donkeys.
B
He named the donkeys Alfa and Beto, which together make the Spanish word for alphabet. Each weekend he walked them into the hills with about 120 books strapped to their backs.
C
A child could keep a book for a week. Soriano wrote the loans in a notebook. Almost every book came back.
D
He kept going for more than twenty years, through heat, rain, and one robbery. A broken leg from a fall did not stop him either.
E
Other places copied the idea. There are book boats in Bangladesh, camel libraries in Kenya, and a book bicycle in the Philippines.
F
All of them solve the same problem in the same way. If people cannot reach the library, the library travels.

title: How Ice Cream Freezes

p: A
Ice cream is mostly cream, sugar, and air. Getting all three to hold together is harder than it sounds.
B
If you froze cream in a cup, you would get a solid block. The water in it would form large ice crystals, and large crystals feel gritty on the tongue.
C
So ice cream is stirred the whole time it freezes. Stirring breaks the crystals before they can grow. Smaller crystals mean a smoother scoop.
D
Stirring also folds in air. A good ice cream is about a quarter air by volume. Without it, the frozen mix would be too hard to scoop.
E
Sugar does something else. Sugar water freezes at a lower temperature than plain water, so some of the mix stays soft even in a freezer.
F
That is why ice cream can be scooped at a temperature where a block of ice would be solid stone.

connection
Describe the connection between sugar and ice cream staying soft.

B

C
Sweden had two choices: stop the mine, which employs most of the town, or move the town. It chose to move the town.
D
The move began in 2014 and will take decades. The new center sits two miles east. Some buildings were pulled down and rebuilt. Others were lifted whole onto trailers and driven.
E
The wooden church, built in 1912 and voted the most beautiful building in Sweden, was cut into pieces and carried in a slow parade to its new place.
F

relocate: To relocate is to move something to a new place.

title: The Bird That Sews

p: A
Most birds build nests by piling things up. The tailorbird does something else. It sews.
B
The bird finds a large green leaf still growing on a branch. Using its beak, it punches a row of small holes along both edges.
C
Then it pulls plant fiber or spider silk through the holes, one hole at a time, and knots the ends so the thread will not slip back out.
D
The leaf folds into a pocket. The bird lines the inside with soft grass and lays its eggs there.
E
Because the leaf is still alive and still attached, it stays green. From a few feet away the nest looks like an ordinary leaf, which is exactly the point.
F
A tailorbird weighs less than a slice of bread. It cannot fight off a snake. Hiding is the whole defense.

title: The Clock That Runs on Water

p: A
Long before gears and springs, people told time with water. A water clock is a jar that leaks on purpose.
B
The simplest kind is a bowl with a small hole in the bottom, floating in a larger basin. Water seeps in, the bowl sinks, and the time it takes to sink is always the same.
C
Egyptian water clocks worked the other way. A jar with markings inside slowly drained, and the falling water level showed the hour.
D
There is a problem. Water drains faster when the jar is full, because the weight above pushes harder. So the early hours ran short and the late hours ran long.
E
Clockmakers solved it by shaping the jar. If the jar is wider at the top, the level falls slowly at first, and the hours come out even.
F
That shape was worked out more than three thousand years ago by people who had no way to measure pressure. They found it by trying.
